record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: Can defenses such as data sanitization and network pruning be adapted to federated learning in a way that does not require direct access to private client data, and how should the gap between data poisoning and model-update poisoning attacks be quantified under realistic federated adversary capabilities?

evidence.quote: Neither data sanitization nor network pruning work directly in federated settings, as they both generally require access to client data, or else data that resembles client data. Thus, it is an open question whether data sanitization methods and network pruning methods can be used in federated settings without privacy loss, or whether or not defenses against data poisoning require new federated approaches. ... One interesting line of study would be to quantify the gap between these two types of attacks, and relate this gap to the relative strength of an adversary operating under these attack models.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates the training of a global model with parameters $	heta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ across $N$ clients. In each round $t$, the server broadcasts the current model $	heta_t$, a subset $S_t \subseteq \{1,\dots,N\}$ of clients each compute an update $\Delta_i^{(t)}$ from their private local dataset $D_i$, and the server aggregates these updates to obtain $	heta_{t+1} = 	heta_t + \mathrm{Agg} igl(\{\Delta_i^{(t)}\}_{i \in S_t} igr)$. The server cannot observe the client data $D_i$ nor any data drawn from the same distribution.

Two classes of adversarial behavior are considered for a fraction $ho$ of compromised clients:
(i) Data poisoning: the adversary alters the local dataset $D_i$ but the client otherwise follows the prescribed local training protocol, producing $\Delta_i^{(t)}$ honestly from the corrupted data.
(ii) Model-update poisoning: the adversary may submit any vector $\Delta_i^{(t)} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ subject to specified constraints (e.g., norm bounds or stealth constraints), without regard to any underlying dataset.

Two standard centralized defenses are:
- Data sanitization: filter or relabel training points by detecting outliers in the training data using a reference (clean) dataset.
- Network pruning: identify and remove neurons or weights that activate primarily on backdoored or anomalous inputs, using clean validation data to detect such neurons.

Both defenses, in their classical forms, require direct access to (a sample of) clean training data resembling the clients' data.

Resolve the following:

(A) Design and analyze data-sanitization-style and network-pruning-style defenses that operate in the federated setting under the constraint that the server has no access to clients' private data and no auxiliary dataset drawn from their distribution, while preserving formally stated privacy guarantees (e.g., $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy with respect to each $D_i$). Provide either (a) provable robustness guarantees—bounds on the deviation $\|	heta_T - 	heta_T^{\mathrm{clean}}\|$ or on the test risk under a specified poisoning model—matching those of the centralized analogues, or (b) impossibility results showing that the centralized guarantees cannot be achieved by any defense satisfying the stated privacy constraint, thereby establishing whether genuinely new federated-specific defenses against data poisoning are required.

(B) Formulate a quantitative measure $G(\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{data}}, \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{model}})$ of the gap between the worst-case attack success achievable by a data-poisoning adversary $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{data}}$ and a model-update-poisoning adversary $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{model}}$ operating under matched, realistic capability budgets (fraction $ho$ of corrupted clients, bounds on per-client update norm, knowledge of other clients' data and of the aggregation rule, computational budget). Prove upper and lower bounds on $G$ as a function of these capability parameters and the aggregation rule $\mathrm{Agg}$, and relate $G$ to a precise notion of relative adversarial strength between the two threat models.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem remains broadly open. Although since 2020 numerous federated defenses have appeared (FoolsGold, robust aggregation rules, anomaly-detection-based filtering, federated data sanitization variants such as FDSD, pruning-style backdoor mitigation), there is no defense that simultaneously matches centralized data-sanitization/network-pruning guarantees while provably respecting client privacy, and recent work continues to break state-of-the-art defenses with optimization-based attacks. No widely accepted quantitative theory of the data-poisoning vs. model-update-poisoning gap under matched federated capabilities has been established.

status_evidence.title: Anomaly detection and defense techniques in federated learning: a comprehensive review
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys defense mechanisms including pruning, data sanitization, robust aggregation, anomaly detection, noting ongoing privacy-utility-robustness tradeoffs.
status_evidence.claim: As of 2024, federated defenses adapting sanitization/pruning are still under active investigation without consensus solutions.

status_evidence.title: Breaking State-of-the-Art Poisoning Defenses to Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: An optimization-based attack framework that defeats current state-of-the-art poisoning defenses in FL.
status_evidence.claim: Existing federated poisoning defenses remain vulnerable, indicating the defense problem is not solved.

status_evidence.title: Federated Learning Attacks Revisited: A Critical Discussion of Gaps, Assumptions, and Evaluation Setups
status_evidence.snippet: Highlights gaps in evaluation and threat-model assumptions for FL poisoning attacks/defenses.
status_evidence.claim: The relative strength of data- vs. model-update-poisoning adversaries in FL is not yet rigorously quantified.
